木琴以琴槌敲擊調音木條發聲，屬體鳴樂器。管弦樂中的木琴音域較馬林巴高，音色較乾；: The xylophone sounds when mallets strike tuned wooden bars, and it is an idiophone. In the orchestra the xylophone sits higher in range than the marimba and sounds drier; a concert xylophone has tubular resonators under the bars, which strengthen the tone and the sustain. Some modern Western xylophones have a range as small as two and a half octaves, while concert instruments usually have three and a half or four octaves, and the part is written an octave below where it sounds. Synthetic materials can be louder; very hard rubber, polyball or acrylic mallets are the norm, while medium-hard rubber, yarn or wooden heads give a softer, lighter tone. Traditional African xylophones resonate through gourds, and adjusting the height of the bars and the mouth of the gourd can amplify the sound; the gil covers small holes with spider silk to produce a buzzing timbre, while the amadinda has no such buzz. The glockenspiel sounds from metal bars and is not a xylophone.
木琴可見於管弦樂團的半音階編制，也見於西方兒童樂器與亞洲、非洲的五聲或七聲音階傳: The xylophone appears in the chromatic line-up of the orchestra, and also among Western children's instruments and in the pentatonic or heptatonic traditions of Asia and Africa. In Southeast Asia it enters the gamelan ensemble and is used on occasions such as the Toba Batak music of northern Sumatra and the pattala of Burma. In Africa it appears in East African xylophone ensembles, in the large ensembles and choreographed dances of the Chopi of Mozambique, in the funeral duets of the Dagara of Ghana and Burkina Faso, and in rituals such as the kazanga and the kuomboka of Zambia.

The xylophone is an idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 111.212, and belongs to the percussion family: it consists of wooden bars struck with mallets, each bar tuned to a pitch of the scale. Traditional xylophones of Asia, Southeast Asia and Africa mostly use a pentatonic or heptatonic scale, Western children's instruments commonly a diatonic one, and the orchestra uses a chromatic xylophone. The player strikes the bars with hard mallets; some African and Southeast Asian instruments resonate through gourds, and are used on occasions such as royal ceremonies, funerals, dances and ensembles.
木琴發聲體多為木條，現代西方琴用玫瑰木、紫檀、可可波羅木或玻璃纖維、玻璃纖維強化: The sounding bodies of the xylophone are mostly wooden bars: modern Western instruments use rosewood, padauk, cocobolo or fibreglass and glass-fibre-reinforced plastic, while some in Southeast Asia are made of bamboo. The frame is wood or steel tubing, and resonators may be gourds or calabash shells, tuned with beeswax or spider silk; African instruments are fixed with antelope sinew and leather. Mallet heads may be hard rubber, acrylic, yarn or wood; wooden mallets are rosewood, ebony or birch, and historical ones willow.
木琴起源不明。Nettl 認為它源於東南亞，約公元五百年隨南島語族遷徙傳入非洲，: The origin of the xylophone is unknown. Nettl held that it came from Southeast Asia and reached Africa around 500 CE with the migration of Austronesian speakers, and he compared East African xylophone ensembles with the gamelan of Java and Bali. Roger Blench argues instead for an independent African origin, on the grounds that the African xylophone has distinctive features and that Africa has more types of xylophone and xylophone-like instruments. The earliest evidence in Southeast Asia is ninth-century; there are also hanging wooden instruments that the Vienna Symphonic Library says appear in what is now China in the second millennium BCE. Early African forms set the bars on gourds and developed interlocking rhythms. Forms and ensemble traditions then diverged in Indonesia, the Malay world, Melanesia, Thailand, Burma, parts of the Americas and across Africa.
站於木琴前，雙手持棒。敲擊琴鍵中央產生音高。音階排列類似鋼琴鍵盤。練習音階上下行: Stand in front of the xylophone with a mallet in each hand. Strike the centre of a bar to produce its pitch. The layout of the scale resembles a piano keyboard. Practise scales up and down, and arpeggios. Choosing mallets of the right hardness affects the timbre.
